stories.title: Demand response in DC microgrids using particle swarm optimization-optimized model predictive control
stories.description: Efficient energy management in DC microgrids requires advanced control strategies capable of handling renewable variability, storage limitations, and dynamic load demands. The proposed strategy employs a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)-tuned custom cost function within Model Predictive Control (MPC) to implement demand response. The controller tracks the uncurtailed demand reference outside scheduled curtailment windows and permits targeted demand reduction within them. The baseline demand profile is treated as the uncurtailed service reference, and demand response is implemented as a scheduled and controlled deviation from that reference rather than as continuous load minimization. The study also provides a structural comparison between the default fixed-weight MPC cost function and the PSO-tuned, mode-dependent custom cost function, interpreting their weights through the control priorities they encode among load tracking, grid use, and hybrid-storage operation. PSO is applied offline to determine two mode-dependent weight sets, while the online MPC uses these fixed weights to respond to changing load and renewable-generation conditions. Simulations under sunny and cloudy conditions show that the custom formulation preserves baseline demand tracking outside the demand-response windows and enables targeted curtailment within them. Quantitatively, the scheduled demand is reduced by 56.4–$$61.0\%$$ during the morning curtailment periods and by $$58.4\%$$ during the afternoon periods, while the tracking error remains below $$1.6\%$$ outside the demand-response windows. Net grid-energy exchange decreases by $$64.3\%$$ under sunny conditions and $$24.1\%$$ under cloudy conditions, and net daily electricity cost decreases by $$49.1\%$$ and $$29.5\%$$, respectively, while both storage states remain within their prescribed limits.

stories.title: Probing the thermoelectric properties of the 8-16-4 graphyne monolayer via tight-binding approach
stories.description: In this study, we explore the thermoelectric specifications of the newly proposed 8–16–4 graphyne lattice (GY) by the tight-binding model (TBM) in combination with Green’s function formalism (GFF). The study focuses on how magnetic field, doping, and strain influence key transport parameters, including electrical and thermal conductivity, and Seebeck coefficient. The calculated electronic density of states reveals a Dirac-like semi-metallic behavior, characterized by a vanishing density near the Fermi level. Our results show that applying compressive strain significantly alters the magnitude and position of the conductivity peaks, demonstrating the tunability of transport properties through lattice deformation. The consistently positive value of the Seebeck coefficient throughout the studied temperature window confirms that holes are the primary contributors to thermoelectric transport. However, when viewed as a function of chemical potential, it undergoes a sign change near the neutrality point, signaling a transition between p-type and n-type transport channels. Furthermore, the magnetic field modifies the peak intensity in the electronic states without affecting their position, underscoring the robustness of the band structure. These findings highlight the potential of 8–16–4 GY as a mechanically flexible and thermoelectrically active two-dimensional (2D) material, suitable for applications in nanoelectronic devices and energy conversion technologies.
